question: You check a mum on her 3rd day after birth. Where do you expect to feel her fundus?

options.A: Completely hidden in the pelvic cavity
options.B: About three fingerbreadths below the umbilicus
options.C: Level with the umbilicus
options.D: Midway between the pubic bone and umbilicus

explanation: You're learning fast! Since the uterus drops by about one fingerbreadth each day after birth, by day three it sits roughly three fingerbreadths below the belly button. Easy to remember on the ward!

question: How does the growing baby and uterus contribute to constipation later in pregnancy?

options.A: By increasing the production of digestive enzymes
options.B: By putting direct mechanical pressure on the bowels
options.C: By completely stopping the production of stomach acid
options.D: By speeding up the movement of food through the colon

explanation: Exactly! As the baby grows, there is less space in the tummy, and the heavy uterus presses right against the intestines, slowing things down.

question: Why is asking about sexual health an important part of routine nursing care?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any laboratory testing
options.B: It ensures compliance with hospital billing policies
options.C: It validates sexual health as a vital component of holistic well-being
options.D: It shortens the overall length of the hospital stay

explanation: Nursing is about caring for the whole person body and mind. Addressing intimate health ensures we look at quality of life, not just curing an illness.

question: When is a patient usually switched from a first-line ART regimen to a second-line regimen?

options.A: Whenever the patient travels to a different state
options.B: After the patient has taken their medication for exactly one month
options.C: When treatment failure is confirmed by a persistently high viral load
options.D: As soon as the patient reports a mild headache

explanation: Spot on! If a patient takes their drugs well, but lab tests keep showing a high viral load, it means the first drugs are failing and it's time to switch regimens.

question: What is a major risk when using large amounts of plain tap water for a washout?

options.A: Permanent damage to the upper respiratory tract
options.B: Water intoxication and severe hyponatremia
options.C: Sudden spikes in systemic blood pressure
options.D: Rapid development of iron deficiency anemia

explanation: Plain water can pass through the bowel wall into the bloodstream, diluting vital body salts and causing a dangerous drop in sodium levels.

question: A patient is recovering from major surgery and needs tissue repair. Which energy state is best?

options.A: Positive energy balance
options.B: Zero net energy balance
options.C: Complete metabolic shutdown
options.D: Severe negative energy balance

explanation: Healing takes work! Building new cells and repairing tissues require extra building blocks and calories, so a positive energy balance is just what the patient needs.

question: A newly diagnosed patient wants to start ARVs right away, but tests show they have active meningitis. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Switch the patient to herbal remedies instead of modern drugs
options.B: Refuse to give any counseling because the patient is too sick
options.C: Start the medication immediately without waiting for any other tests
options.D: Support delaying ART briefly while the acute meningitis is treated

explanation: Correct! For serious infections like meningitis, doctors treat the acute infection first before starting ART to prevent dangerous inflammation reactions in the immune system.

question: What heart action directly causes the apex beat you feel on the chest?

options.A: Filling of the right atrium during diastole
options.B: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves
options.C: Contraction of the left ventricle during systole
options.D: Opening of the tricuspid and mitral valves

explanation: When the left ventricle squeezes, it twists forward and taps against the chest wall, creating that palpable apex beat. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h6)

question: Why must the objectives of an explanatory study be very specific?

options.A: To make sure no other nurse can ever replicate the study
options.B: To ensure the research paper is at least one hundred pages long
options.C: To prevent patients from asking questions about the study
options.D: To help the researcher stay focused on finding direct answers and proper statistics

explanation: Exactly! Specific objectives keep your study tightly focused on testing cause and effect without getting distracted.

question: How does stomach pain from a gastric ulcer usually behave compared to a duodenal ulcer?

options.A: Gastric ulcer pain often worsens soon after eating food.
options.B: Gastric ulcer pain is relieved by eating meals.
options.C: Duodenal ulcer pain gets worse immediately during a meal.
options.D: Duodenal ulcer pain never occurs at night.

explanation: Correct! Food triggers acid release, which immediately irritates a gastric ulcer. Duodenal ulcers, on the other hand, often feel better temporarily when food is in the stomach.

question: Why is handing project ownership over to local community members crucial for sustainability?

options.A: So the program continues running even after external funding or staff leave
options.B: So the government can tax the community for health services
options.C: So nobody can be held responsible if the project fails
options.D: So nurses can retire and stop working permanently

explanation: When locals own and lead the initiative, the program survives independently of outside organizations and temporary grants. [learn more](GNS314_U4_T7#GNS314_U4_T7_h8)

question: Why is teamwork among different healthcare professionals so crucial in long-term care?

options.A: Medical doctors require assistance to perform basic personal hygiene
options.B: Residents typically have multiple complex physical, emotional, and social needs
options.C: It ensures that nurses never have to communicate with resident families
options.D: It removes the need for documenting resident care assessments

explanation: Brilliant! Because residents have varied needs, nurses, doctors, dietitians, and therapists must work hand-in-hand to cover all bases.

question: Which official council regulates the practice and licensing of midwives in Nigeria?

options.A: West African Health Community Board
options.B: National Union of Local Government Employees
options.C: Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria
options.D: Medical and Dental Association of Nigeria

explanation: The NMCN is the body that sets our professional standards, trains us, and gives us our licenses to practice safely.

question: How does a community nurse act as a bridge for families?

options.A: By acting as a legal judge in food disputes
options.B: By importing expensive foreign supplements for every home
options.C: By connecting scientific guidelines with the daily realities of households
options.D: By building physical bridges across local rivers for food transport

explanation: Nurses translate complex health information into practical advice that fits what families can actually afford and access. [learn more](GNS227_U3_T003#GNS227_U3_T003_h2)

question: Which serious condition involves tissue damage and inflammation in the bowels of a premature baby?

options.A: Retinopathy of prematurity
options.B: Transient tachypnea of the newborn
options.C: Necrotizing enterocolitis
options.D: Intraventricular hemorrhage

explanation: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is a tough bowel complication in preemies where parts of the intestine can suffer tissue death. You're mastering complex neonatal nursing topics!

question: What is the main job of an enzyme in the body?

options.A: To lower body temperature during a fever
options.B: To speed up the rate of chemical reactions
options.C: To carry oxygen from the lungs to the brain
options.D: To store excess fat in adipose tissues

explanation: Enzymes are like speedy helpers—they act as biological catalysts so vital chemical reactions happen fast enough to keep us going.

question: What happens to urea and other metabolic waste in a healthy nephron?

options.A: They are converted into useful proteins in the loop of Henle
options.B: They are stored in the renal cortex for later energy use
options.C: They are filtered out of the blood and excreted in urine
options.D: They are reabsorbed entirely to nourish kidney tissue

explanation: Exactly! The body doesn't need these wastes, so the nephrons filter them out of the bloodstream so they can leave the body in urine.

question: Which finding around a drainage tube insertion site is a sign of a potential infection?

options.A: Clear pink fluid on the outer dressing
options.B: Purulent discharge and foul odor
options.C: A small amount of dried blood at the stitch
options.D: Soft skin that feels cool to the touch

explanation: Pus and bad smells are classic indicators that bacteria are multiplying at the wound site, signaling a developing infection. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T14#GNS122_U2_T14_h2)

question: Why is nursing care during the puerperium so important for a new mother?

options.A: It ensures the mother avoids all postpartum sadness
options.B: It prevents sudden complications like hemorrhage and infection
options.C: It eliminates the need for any follow-up doctor visits
options.D: It guarantees the infant will sleep through the night

explanation: You've got this! Regular checks in the postpartum period help catch physical problems early, keeping the new mother safe and healthy during her recovery.

question: Why is routine monitoring so helpful on a busy hospital ward?

options.A: It stops patients from ever developing hospital-acquired infections.
options.B: It guarantees that the hospital will receive international funding.
options.C: It helps clinical teams spot operational issues and prevent crises early.
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for any staff performance appraisals.

explanation: When you monitor daily routines, you catch small problems (like running low on supplies) before they turn into major emergencies for your patients. Smart nursing!

question: Why do teenage girls need more dietary iron than young boys of the same age?

options.A: To replace iron lost monthly through menstruation
options.B: To compensate for low carbohydrate intake
options.C: To prevent the rapid onset of adult diabetes
options.D: To build stronger tooth enamel

explanation: That's correct! Regular menstrual blood loss means teenage girls need extra iron in their diet to stay energetic and avoid anemia.

question: Which expense usually takes up the biggest slice of a hospital's budget?

options.A: Patient dietary services
options.B: Office stationery supplies
options.C: Facility security contracts
options.D: Healthcare personnel salaries

explanation: Correct! Paying the dedicated nurses, doctors, and support staff who keep the hospital running takes up the largest share of operating costs.

question: Why is community education just as important as passing laws to stop FGM?

options.A: It allows communities to vote on whether they want to follow federal laws
options.B: It addresses the root cultural beliefs and social norms that sustain the practice
options.C: It ensures that traditional cutters can find alternative paying jobs easily
options.D: It replaces the need for police officers and court systems entirely

explanation: Well done! Laws alone cannot change deeply held mindsets. Education helps communities willingly choose to leave the practice behind.

question: Which health indicator typically gets better as a country's GNP goes up?

options.A: Incidence of waterborne diseases
options.B: Infant mortality rate
options.C: General population morbidity
options.D: Rate of chronic malnutrition

explanation: As a nation grows wealthier, it can afford better maternal and child healthcare, which means fewer babies dying in infancy. Great health systems start with strong economies!

question: Which group of workers faces the highest daily risk of exposure to bloodborne infections like HIV and Hepatitis B?

options.A: Healthcare workers
options.B: Market porters
options.C: Textile weavers
options.D: Construction laborers

explanation: As nurses, doctors, and lab staff handling needles and body fluids daily, we are right on the front line for bloodborne risks.

question: Why must wrapped instrument trays be loaded loosely inside a steam sterilizer?

options.A: To allow steam to circulate freely around every package
options.B: To stop the external indicator tape from melting off
options.C: To prevent the heavy metal trays from breaking the door
options.D: To make unloading faster for the nursing assistant

explanation: If the packs are crammed too tightly together, the steam can't reach every surface, leaving pockets where germs can survive.

question: Which cells in the testes are responsible for producing testosterone?

options.A: Spermatids
options.B: Leydig cells
options.C: Sertoli cells
options.D: Spermatogonia

explanation: Leydig cells are found between the tubules and synthesize the primary male sex hormone, testosterone. [learn more](GNS216_U2_T7#GNS216_U2_T7_h5)

question: Why is helping a vulnerable widow learn a trade and find legal aid a great long-term nursing goal?

options.A: It guarantees that she will never experience grief or sadness again
options.B: It replaces the need for any medical or psychological treatment
options.C: It legally forces the extended family to apologize in public
options.D: It promotes financial independence and protects her against further exploitation

explanation: Money struggles and lack of support often trap widows in abusive cycles. Empowering them helps secure their safety and freedom.

question: How does end-of-life nursing care differ from standard acute hospital care?

options.A: Family members take over all physical nursing duties inside the hospital ward
options.B: Treatment focuses exclusively on aggressive life-support interventions
options.C: Nurses stop monitoring vital signs and administering any form of medication
options.D: Care priorities shift from curing disease to ensuring comfort, dignity, and symptom relief

explanation: When medical cures are no longer possible, our focus shifts beautifully toward peace, pain control, and supporting loved ones through a very tender time.

question: Which of these is a BAD idea when dressing for work in the instrument washing area?

options.A: Fluid-resistant long-sleeved surgical gown
options.B: Open-toed canvas shoes for ventilation and comfort
options.C: Heavy-duty puncture-resistant utility gloves
options.D: Protective face shield or goggles

explanation: Ouch—open shoes are a hazard! They leave your feet completely unprotected against chemical spills, heavy dropped tools, and splashing fluids.

question: Which factor is most critical for ensuring the long-term sustainability of a community health project?

options.A: Total community ownership and local leadership
options.B: Permanent supervision by foreign medical doctors
options.C: Keeping all project funds hidden in a secret bank account
options.D: Banning local meetings after the project is completed

explanation: When a community feels the project belongs to them, they maintain it long after external support ends. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T1#GNS124_U4_T1_h8)

question: Which body language habit helps your patient feel trusted and relaxed during an interview?

options.A: Checking your watch frequently
options.B: Crossing your arms tightly
options.C: Maintaining an open body posture
options.D: Looking away while they speak

explanation: Well done! Keeping an open posture shows your patient you are warm, friendly, and genuinely ready to listen to their story.

question: A patient recovering from serum sickness complains of stiff, aching joints. Which nursing action is best?

options.A: Apply ice packs to the joints for twenty minutes every hour
options.B: Massage the inflamed joint firmly to break up the immune complexes
options.C: Keep the affected limbs strictly immobilized in a rigid splint
options.D: Encourage gentle range-of-motion exercises as tolerated

explanation: Gentle movement is wonderful here; it keeps the joints from locking up while giving the tissues space to heal comfortably.

question: Which feature is essential for adolescent-friendly health services?

options.A: Higher service fees to cover specialized staff
options.B: Strict daytime-only scheduling constraints
options.C: Strict guarantee of client confidentiality
options.D: Mandatory parental presence during exams

explanation: Teens need to trust that their private health matters stay private. Confidentiality builds that crucial bridge!

question: What is your very first nursing action if a patient shows signs of a severe adverse drug reaction?

options.A: Wait until the doctor finishes the ward round
options.B: Ask the patient to sign a refusal of treatment form
options.C: Increase the fluid intake to dilute the drug
options.D: Discontinue the offending medication right away

explanation: Stop the drug first! Cutting off the source is your priority before doing anything else to help.

question: What is the main goal of Clinical Decision Support (CDS) alerts inside an EMR?

options.A: To schedule cleaning staff for patient rooms after discharge
options.B: To warn staff about drug allergies and dangerous interactions
options.C: To lock the computer screen if a nurse steps away too long
options.D: To calculate monthly hospital electricity and water bills

explanation: Think of CDS tools as a friendly safety net. They pop up to give you a heads-up if a prescribed drug clashes with a patient's known allergies.

question: Beyond physical checks, what is another crucial part of postpartum care for a mother who just had twins or triplets?

options.A: Encouraging the mother to return to work within two weeks
options.B: Restricting family visits to prevent the mother from talking
options.C: Providing emotional support and connecting them with practical resources
options.D: Insisting that the mother cares for the newborns entirely on her own

explanation: Well done! Raising more than one baby at once can feel overwhelming. Offering kind words and connecting families to helper networks is a huge part of great nursing care.

question: Patients who walk more steps each day report lower levels of pain. What kind of relationship is this?

options.A: Negative correlation
options.B: Zero correlation
options.C: Positive correlation
options.D: Experimental correlation

explanation: You got it! Higher step counts go hand-in-hand with lower pain levels. Because they move in opposite directions, it's a negative correlation.

question: What is the main benefit of drawing an epidemic curve during an investigation?

options.A: It automatically cures infected patients within the first week.
options.B: It replaces the need for laboratory confirmation of blood samples.
options.C: It helps show how the disease is spreading and when exposure likely happened.
options.D: It proves which specific nurse made the initial error.

explanation: An epidemic curve is simply a graph of symptom timelines. It helps investigators spot patterns and figure out when people first caught the illness.

question: Which of these is NOT a good way to work with traditional healers in a local community?

options.A: Educating them on the danger of delayed hospital treatment
options.B: Insulting their practices publicly to show modern medical superiority
options.C: Inviting them to dialogue meetings to discuss patient safety
options.D: Finding ways to build respectful referral links with them

explanation: Spot on! Publicly shaming traditional practitioners only creates bitterness and drives patients away from getting the formal care they need.

question: In which hospital zone are people allowed to wear regular street clothes?

options.A: Semi-restricted zone
options.B: Restricted zone
options.C: Unrestricted zone
options.D: Sterile core

explanation: Correct! The unrestricted zone is the welcoming entrance area where street clothes are still fine before you move closer to the clean zones.

question: How did later revisions of Nigeria's population policy change compared to the 1988 version?

options.A: They shifted toward a rights-based approach focusing on quality of life.
options.B: They focused exclusively on increasing the total population size.
options.C: They made family planning completely illegal across all states.
options.D: They abandoned all health-related goals to focus solely on taxation.

explanation: Later updates moved away from strict child limits. Instead, they focused on human rights, reproductive health, and helping families live better, sustainable lives.

question: What is reminiscence therapy?

options.A: Forcing a patient to forget painful childhood memories
options.B: Discussing and reflecting on past positive life events
options.C: Administering medication to induce deep sleep
options.D: Practicing physical exercises to improve balance

explanation: Reminiscence therapy uses happy memories to boost mood, self-worth, and comfort. A wonderful, non-drug intervention!

question: Which nursing documentation detail is essential after finishing a gastric lavage session?

options.A: The brand name and factory serial number of the lavage tube
options.B: Total amounts of fluid put in and taken out of the stomach
options.C: The exact weight of the patient measured in kilograms
options.D: The name of the family member who gave consent for care

explanation: Recording fluid balance prevents water intoxication or electrolyte imbalances, confirming that the nurse recovered roughly what was instilled. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h6)

question: Which family planning pill is best for mothers who are breastfeeding in the early months because it won't dry up their milk?

options.A: Menopausal hormone therapy
options.B: Combined estrogen pills
options.C: High-dose emergency pills
options.D: Progestin-only pills

explanation: Progestin-only pills (the 'minipill') are safe for nursing moms because they don't mess with breastmilk production like estrogen can.

question: Which communication technique helps encourage a patient to open up about their feelings?

options.A: Offering false reassurance
options.B: Changing the conversation topic
options.C: Giving immediate advice
options.D: Asking open-ended questions

explanation: Open-ended questions (like 'How have you been sleeping lately?') invite patients to share their story freely instead of just nodding with a simple yes or no.

question: What is the main reason for evaluating an outbreak after it has ended?

options.A: To learn from response strengths and weaknesses to improve future preparedness
options.B: To increase taxes on communities that experienced high infection rates
options.C: To punish health workers who made mistakes during the emergency peak
options.D: To permanently close down the healthcare facilities that treated patients

explanation: Post-outbreak reviews help our health systems learn what went right and what to fix before the next emergency hits.

question: Why did medicine shift from using whole plants to isolating just the active ingredients?

options.A: To make the medicines taste sweet for children
options.B: Because crude plants have zero medicinal value
options.C: To make sure every dose is exact and safe
options.D: Because plants became completely extinct globally

explanation: Plants can vary in strength depending on the season. Isolating the active chemical lets us give a safe, precise dose every single time.

question: Why must nurses balance medical treatments with a resident's personal wishes?

options.A: To avoid documenting any clinical changes in the chart.
options.B: To ensure the patient performs all physical therapy alone.
options.C: To respect resident dignity while still achieving safe, effective outcomes.
options.D: To completely bypass hospital discharge regulations.

explanation: Person-centered care means we team up with our patients, respecting what they value while keeping them safe and healthy. You're doing great!

question: Where are surgical family planning procedures, like tubal ligation, usually performed?

options.A: Secondary or tertiary hospital
options.B: Mobile immunization outreach post
options.C: Primary health post
options.D: Community pharmacy shop

explanation: Major surgeries need sterile operating theatres and specialized surgical teams found in our bigger hospitals.

question: Who should be cared for using standard precautions in a hospital?

options.A: Every patient, regardless of their diagnosis
options.B: Patients admitted to surgical wards only
options.C: Only patients with confirmed viral infections
options.D: Only individuals coughing or showing rashes

explanation: Standard precautions are universal and must be applied to all patients because infection status is not always known upfront. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T16#GNS122_U2_T16_h4)

question: What is a common research duty for a bedside staff nurse?

options.A: Collecting data and identifying study participants
options.B: Funding major multi-center clinical drug trials
options.C: Writing national health policy legislation
options.D: Publishing textbooks for medical schools

explanation: Bedside nurses are closest to patients, making them well-suited to spot eligible participants and gather accurate clinical data. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T5#GNS217_U2_T5_h2)

question: Why is smoking a cigarette near oxygen therapy a massive fire hazard?

options.A: Smokers are unable to handle oxygen equipment properly
options.B: Oxygen tanks release toxic gases when heated by smoke
options.C: Cigarettes automatically explode when they touch oxygen tubing
options.D: Oxygen feeds fires and makes flames spread with explosive speed

explanation: Medical oxygen makes fires burn super fast and extremely hot. Even a small spark near oxygen can turn into a dangerous blaze instantly.

question: Why is dry, cracked skin from frequent hand washing a big concern for nurses?

options.A: It prevents the nurses from wearing sterile gloves properly
options.B: Cracked, dry skin harbors more bacteria and increases infection risks
options.C: It makes the skin look unprofessional during ward rounds
options.D: It stops alcohol rubs from evaporating correctly

explanation: Tiny cracks in dry skin create cozy hiding spots for bacteria, which defeats the whole purpose of washing. Remember to use hand cream!

question: What makes a 'prodrug' unique compared to regular medicines?

options.A: It is always given as a liquid injection rather than a pill
options.B: It bypasses the liver completely without ever changing form
options.C: It is given in an inactive form and needs metabolism to become active
options.D: It leaves the body immediately through sweat instead of urine

explanation: A prodrug is like an undercover agent—it starts off inactive when you swallow it, and only wakes up (becomes active) after the body's metabolism works on it. Pretty cool, right?

question: Why does the standard physical assessment order change when examining a patient's abdomen?

options.A: Palpating too early can alter natural bowel sounds
options.B: Percussion must happen before looking at the skin
options.C: Inspection is completely unnecessary for abdominal exams
options.D: Auscultation is always painful for the patient

explanation: Pressing or pushing on the abdomen stimulates peristalsis, which would give you false readings when you try to listen to bowel sounds afterward. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T3#GNS123_U2_T3_h4)

question: Which type of feedback mechanism is most common for maintaining normal daily physiological ranges?

options.A: Negative feedback
options.B: Neutral feedback
options.C: Additive feedback
options.D: Positive feedback

explanation: Negative feedback is the most common control mechanism because it counteracts deviations to keep body systems stable. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T10#GNS111_U1_T10_h3)

question: A child eats enough daily calories from starchy grains like maize or cassava, but still has severe anemia. What economic factor is likely behind this?

options.A: Too much household spending on medical insurance
options.B: Inability to afford protein and micronutrient-dense foods
options.C: High local agricultural productivity driving down grain value
options.D: Excessive availability of fresh vegetables in local markets

explanation: Getting enough calories for energy isn't the same as getting rich nutrients. Without money for protective foods, deficiencies like anemia happen.

question: How does Behavioural Change Communication (BCC) differ from basic health education?

options.A: BCC focuses on active behavior change rather than just sharing information
options.B: Basic health education involves no communication at all
options.C: BCC is only used inside tertiary hospitals by doctors
options.D: Basic education is meant for children while BCC is for adults

explanation: Think of it this way: health education gives people the facts, but BCC goes a step further to help them actually overcome personal and social barriers to take action. You're building solid community nursing foundations!

question: Why can it be extra challenging to build trust with patients who have illness anxiety?

options.A: They are physically incapable of speaking with medical staff
options.B: They often feel dismissed or ridiculed by providers in the past
options.C: They refuse to answer any questions about their family history
options.D: They only communicate through written letters and notes

explanation: Since past clinicians may have brushed them off with 'there is nothing wrong with you,' these patients expect nurses to disbelieve their real emotional pain.

question: Who is known as the father of nutrition for his early work on how our bodies use oxygen to burn food for energy?

options.A: James Lind
options.B: Casimir Funk
options.C: Antoine Lavoisier
options.D: Hippocrates

explanation: Correct! Lavoisier used clever chemical experiments to show how respiration and metabolism tie directly into how we process food.

question: Why were some people initially hesitant about modern family planning programs in Nigeria?

options.A: A total lack of trained nurses in every region of the country
options.B: Strict government bans on building hospitals and clinics
options.C: Cultural norms, religious beliefs, and mistrust of population policies
options.D: The complete absence of traditional birth spacing methods

explanation: Because these programs were newly introduced, many communities viewed them with suspicion, worrying about foreign population control motives.

question: Your patient's blood glucose is still dangerously high despite your nursing interventions. What should you do next?

options.A: Remove all diabetes education materials from the chart
options.B: Collaborate with the healthcare team to revise the care plan
options.C: Discharge the patient immediately because goals were achieved
options.D: Document that the patient refused to cooperate with therapy

explanation: Well done! If the goal isn't met, nursing isn't over. You team up with the doctors and colleagues to try a new, better approach.

question: How do typical skin lesions of Kaposi sarcoma look?

options.A: Painful, red ulcers with a yellow base
options.B: Itchy, fluid-filled vesicular clusters
options.C: Scaly, silvery plaques with dry edges
options.D: Painless, purplish or brownish nodules

explanation: Skin lesions from Kaposi sarcoma usually show up as distinct, firm, and painless spots or bumps that look purple, pink, or brown.

question: What is your duty as a nurse regarding a patient's feelings and mindset during a referral?

options.A: Counseling the patient to address fears and explain why care is needed
options.B: Telling the family to ignore advice given by the receiving doctor
options.C: Forcing the patient to leave the clinic immediately without explanation
options.D: Convincing the patient that the local clinic can handle everything

explanation: Wonderful nursing care! Taking time to talk, soothe fears, and explain things helps the patient trust the process and actually go for their treatment.

question: What does arterial bleeding typically look like?

options.A: Clear fluid mixed with streaks of old blood
options.B: Slowly oozing blood that stops without pressure
options.C: Bright red blood that spurts with each heartbeat
options.D: Dark red blood that flows in a steady stream

explanation: Arteries carry oxygenated blood under high pressure straight from the heart, causing it to spurt when they are cut. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T4#GNS123_U3_T4_h2)

question: What is considered the gold standard method for measuring energy expenditure in a clinical setting?

options.A: Indirect calorimetry
options.B: Standard height-weight charts
options.C: Bioelectrical impedance
options.D: Skinfold caliper testing

explanation: Indirect calorimetry is a neat clinical test that calculates metabolic rate by analyzing the oxygen a patient inhales and the carbon dioxide they exhale.

question: A patient with a history of stomach ulcers has joint pain. Which drug group should make you extra careful as a nurse?

options.A: Central nervous system sedatives
options.B: Opioid pain medications
options.C: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
options.D: Co-analgesic nerve medications

explanation: NSAIDs (like ibuprofen) block protective factors in the stomach lining. For a patient with ulcers, this can easily trigger bleeding!

question: Why is proper cold chain management especially challenging in rural Nigerian healthcare settings?

options.A: Unreliable electricity supply and high ambient temperatures
options.B: Vaccines manufactured locally do not require refrigeration
options.C: An overabundance of modern refrigerated transport trucks
options.D: Lack of community interest in preventive health services

explanation: Erratic power grids and hot weather make keeping vaccines cold a constant logistical hurdle for rural healthcare workers. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T8#GNS313_U1_T8_h7)

question: Why is the nursing history an essential part of a comprehensive assessment?

options.A: It provides vital details about the child's developmental timeline and home environment
options.B: It replaces the need for laboratory investigations
options.C: It diagnoses rare genetic disorders without testing
options.D: It is only used for billing and insurance purposes

explanation: Parents share daily observations that help nurses and doctors understand the full picture of the child's health. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T6#GNS225_U5_T6_h3)

question: What type of diet is usually given to a patient on the day before a barium enema?

options.A: Clear liquid diet
options.B: Low-residue solid diet
options.C: High-fiber soft diet
options.D: Full regular diet

explanation: A clear liquid diet leaves very little solid waste in the digestive tract, which keeps the colon nice and clean for the imaging.

question: A lucid adult patient refuses to take their morning drugs. What should you do first?

options.A: Explore the patient's reasons, explain the risks of refusal, and inform the doctor.
options.B: Crush the pills into the patient's breakfast porridge so they swallow them unknowingly.
options.C: Document that the patient is non-compliant and ignore them for the rest of the shift.
options.D: Threaten to discharge the patient immediately if they do not cooperate with care.

explanation: Spot on! Patients have a right to choose. Take time to listen to their worries, educate them on the risks, and keep the medical team in the loop.

question: Why is it risky to think of urine leaking as just a normal part of getting older?

options.A: It causes severe skin rashes in all elderly people
options.B: It stops patients from seeking helpful treatment
options.C: It automatically leads to kidney failure
options.D: It means the bladder has completely stopped working

explanation: When patients or their families think leaking is just normal aging, they keep quiet and miss out on treatments that could really help them feel better. Great insight for a nurse!

question: A patient takes a standard drug dose, but it doesn't work because their liver enzymes break it down way faster than usual. What is this patient called?

options.A: Ultrarapid metabolizer
options.B: Poor metabolizer
options.C: First-pass blocker
options.D: Renal excretory failure

explanation: An 'ultrarapid metabolizer' clears drugs out of their system so fast that standard doses vanish before they can therapeutic effects. Pharmacology keeps getting more interesting!

question: What is an example of a direct health injury caused straight away by an earthquake?

options.A: A stroke caused by missed blood pressure pills
options.B: Crush injuries from a collapsed roof
options.C: Depression months after losing a home
options.D: A cholera outbreak from bad drinking water

explanation: Direct injuries happen right at the moment of the event, like getting hit by falling blocks. You're building solid clinical instincts!

question: Which of these describes euthanasia?

options.A: A clinician directly administers a lethal substance to end the patient's life
options.B: High doses of pain medication are given purely to make the patient sleep
options.C: A patient takes a prescribed lethal medication on their own
options.D: Doctors stop giving food and water to a dying patient

explanation: In euthanasia, a doctor or healthcare provider takes the active, direct step of administering a lethal substance to end a suffering patient's life.

question: A diabetic patient needs a clear fluid diet after surgery. What should you look out for?

options.A: Provide regular sweetened fruit juices to boost immediate energy.
options.B: Withhold all fluids until insulin can be completely stopped.
options.C: Ensure the patient receives sugar-free clear liquid options.
options.D: Allow the patient to eat any sweet full fluid item desired.

explanation: Even on liquid diets, blood sugar control matters. Always reach for sugar-free options to keep their glucose stable.

question: What is a key way a nurse advocates for a patient with poorly controlled pain?

options.A: Checking vital signs and ignoring what the patient says
options.B: Telling the patient to endure the pain so they don't get used to drugs
options.C: Waiting until the patient begs for stronger medicine
options.D: Working with the doctor to update an ineffective pain plan

explanation: As a nurse, you are the patient's voice. If their current medication isn't working, speak up and collaborate with the medical team to find a better solution!

question: Why is using real data better than relying only on gut feeling during quality improvement?

options.A: Data processing is legally mandated for every single patient interaction
options.B: Data completely eliminates the need for experienced clinical staff
options.C: Data analysis is always faster than talking to patients on the ward
options.D: Data provides an objective factual reality and avoids personal bias

explanation: Our gut feelings can sometimes trick us or be biased. Clear data gives us the honest, unvarnished truth about what is happening in patient care!

question: Why is regular evaluation of objectives important for a healthcare unit?

options.A: It automatically increases the hospital's annual profits
options.B: It ensures that nurses never have to write care plans again
options.C: It stops patients from asking questions about their treatment
options.D: It allows managers to spot falling performance and adjust tactics early

explanation: Monitoring lets teams catch issues and fix processes before small problems turn into major safety failures. [learn more](GST321_U2_T3#GST321_U2_T3_h7)

question: Which of these best describes the labia minora?

options.A: They are delicate, hairless skin folds
options.B: They are thick pads of fatty tissue
options.C: They produce mature ova
options.D: They cover the pubic symphysis

explanation: Well done! The labia minora are the thin, smooth folds found just inside the labia majora.

question: Your clinic has free cholera vaccines, but villagers are refusing them because of scary rumours. What should you do?

options.A: Close the clinic permanently and transfer the nursing staff to a city
options.B: Use BCC strategies like town hall meetings to address rumors and build trust
options.C: Call the police to force every single villager to receive the injection
options.D: Ignore the rumours and wait for people to figure out the truth alone

explanation: Exactly! Open dialogue and town hall meetings help clear up dangerous myths and build confidence in public health care.

question: Why is primary health care considered a philosophy rather than just a place to treat sick people?

options.A: It guides how entire societies approach social justice and wellness
options.B: It forbids the use of modern pharmaceutical medications
options.C: It requires all nurses to hold a university degree in philosophy
options.D: It focuses exclusively on treating mental health conditions

explanation: Think of primary health care as a mindset! It's an entire value system centered on fairness, community involvement, and stopping illness before it even starts.

question: How do restrictive lung disorders mainly affect how the lungs work?

options.A: They trap large volumes of stale air inside the alveoli
options.B: They increase airway resistance specifically during expiration
options.C: They decrease the total capacity and expansion of the lungs
options.D: They lower the heart rate to slow down blood circulation

explanation: You're doing great! Restrictive disorders make the lung tissue or chest wall stiff, so the lungs just cannot expand to hold a normal volume of air. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T9#GNS213_U2_T9_h2)

question: A community health nurse notices that pregnant women in her area always arrive late with severe complications. What is the best proactive step to take?

options.A: Wait until the government builds a new tertiary hospital nearby
options.B: Report the patients to local traditional rulers for punishment
options.C: Refuse to treat patients who arrive after their expected due date
options.D: Conduct community education on pregnancy danger signs and early clinic attendance

explanation: Proactive education is key! Teaching women about danger signs before complications arise helps them recognize trouble early and come to the clinic on time.

question: What is the main benefit of waste minimization in a health care setting?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any waste bins
options.B: It speeds up the process of patient admission
options.C: It reduces overall risk and treatment costs
options.D: It stops patients from getting hospital infections

explanation: Producing less waste means fewer hazardous materials require expensive and complex treatment processes. [learn more](GST114_U6_T12#GST114_U6_T12_h3)

question: How many unique patient identifiers should a nurse check before giving medication?

options.A: Only one
options.B: At least two
options.C: Exactly four
options.D: None if the nurse knows the patient well

explanation: Using at least two patient identifiers, such as checking the hospital band and asking the patient's name, ensures the correct person receives the medication. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h5)

question: What is the main goal of home health care?

options.A: To provide permanent housing for chronically ill elderly citizens
options.B: To train family members to take over all doctor responsibilities
options.C: To deliver professional nursing and medical services directly to a patient's residence
options.D: To completely replace the need for emergency room visits during major trauma

explanation: Spot on! Home health care brings clinical nursing straight to the patient's doorstep to help them heal comfortably where they live.

question: In chronic kidney disease, why do we need to restrict foods that are high in phosphorus?

options.A: To stop the sudden accumulation of excess stomach acid
options.B: To stimulate healthy red blood cell production in the bone marrow
options.C: To reduce the frequency of painful urinary tract infections
options.D: To prevent bone disease and dangerous vascular calcification

explanation: Failing kidneys struggle to clear phosphorus. Excess phosphorus steals calcium from the bones and hardens blood vessels, which spells trouble for the heart.

question: To diagnose Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD), how long must a patient experience excessive, hard-to-control worry?

options.A: One year
options.B: Six months
options.C: One month
options.D: Two weeks

explanation: Correct! For a GAD diagnosis, the persistent worry needs to span at least six months. Keep up the brilliant study habit!

question: How do sebum (skin oil) and sweat team up to protect your body?

options.A: They combine to form an acid mantle that stops germs from growing.
options.B: They cool down internal organs by freezing surface blood vessels.
options.C: They create a thick physical padding against heavy bumps.
options.D: They digest food particles absorbed through the skin.

explanation: Exactly! Sebum and sweat mix on the skin to create the acid mantle, turning the skin into a tough environment for germs. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h3)

question: What type of organism causes yellow fever?

options.A: A protozoan
options.B: A bacterium
options.C: A virus
options.D: A fungus

explanation: Yellow fever is an acute viral disease caused by a member of the Flaviviridae family. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T9#GNS214_U1_T9_h1)

question: What is the best way to document a skin lesion in a patient's chart?

options.A: Sketch the lesion on scrap paper and leave it unrecorded in charts
options.B: Use precise measurements, anatomical locations, and objective descriptive terms
options.C: Use general labels like 'large sore' to save time during documentation
options.D: Write brief personal opinions regarding the patient's personal hygiene

explanation: Be specific! Writing exact sizes, locations, and clear descriptions helps other nurses track if the wound is healing properly.

question: What term describes how consistent and repeatable a research measurement tool is?

options.A: Randomization
options.B: External validity
options.C: Selection bias
options.D: Reliability

explanation: If a tool is reliable, you can trust it to give you consistent results every single time you use it, no matter who is holding it.

question: What happens to most people who catch the poliovirus?

options.A: They experience severe respiratory failure
options.B: They show no symptoms at all
options.C: They suffer from chronic diarrhea
options.D: They develop permanent paralysis

explanation: Surprise! The vast majority of people infected with polio feel completely fine, which is why it can spread so silently in communities.

question: When does a nurse actually begin assessing a client's respiratory status?

options.A: Only after listening to the posterior chest
options.B: When the client complains of chest pain
options.C: After checking the client's laboratory results
options.D: The moment the nurse first sees the client

explanation: Initial visual inspection begins immediately upon meeting the client, noting posture, breathing effort, and skin color before any formal exam starts. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T2#GNS213_U2_T2_h1)

question: How does cultural stigma affect the two-way referral process?

options.A: It ensures that primary health clinics receive adequate funding from local chiefs
options.B: It delays initial professional help-seeking, often bringing clients to the hospital only in severe crises
options.C: It makes downward referral unnecessary because clients recover faster at home
options.D: It encourages families to maintain smooth communication with tertiary psychiatrists

explanation: Because of stigma, families often try other options first. By the time they reach the hospital, the illness has usually progressed to a crisis.

question: Which disease category needs to be reported immediately within 24 hours because it can spark a fast epidemic?

options.A: Category 3
options.B: Category 1
options.C: Category 2
options.D: Category 4

explanation: Spot on! Category 1 diseases are serious emergencies that require instant notification—sometimes with a quick phone call right away.

question: What does medication adherence mean in nursing practice?

options.A: The doctor writes prescriptions without making spelling errors
options.B: The pharmacy delivers medications to the hospital on time
options.C: The nurse stores drugs safely inside the medication trolley
options.D: The patient takes their prescribed drugs correctly and consistently

explanation: Adherence refers to how closely a patient follows the agreed-upon medication schedule in daily life. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T3#GNS125_U3_T3_h6)

question: What is a common operational challenge faced by nurses in Nigerian primary health care centers?

options.A: Shortages of essential medications and unreliable power supply
options.B: Constant availability of high-tech diagnostic equipment
options.C: Too many advanced surgical specialists on site
options.D: Excessive funding and overstaffing of rural clinics

explanation: Basic infrastructure deficits and supply shortages are common operational challenges in many primary health centers. [learn more](GNS124_U2_T7#GNS124_U2_T7_h8)

question: What is the purpose of food security early warning systems?

options.A: To predict exact rainfall amounts for the next ten years
options.B: To stop international trade negotiations permanently
options.C: To warn citizens about high prices in luxury restaurants
options.D: To detect impending food shortages before famine strikes

explanation: Early warning systems monitor data so authorities can respond before a crisis becomes a full-scale famine. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T028#GNS227_U2_T028_h7)

question: Why do health NGOs often experience high staff turnover?

options.A: Clinics close down every few months due to weather
options.B: Staff members are legally required to change jobs yearly
options.C: They often rely on short-term contracts and lower pay
options.D: Government hospitals steal all qualified nurses by force

explanation: That's right! Because funding comes in short bursts, NGOs often can't offer permanent jobs with great pay, so staff look for stable work elsewhere. [learn more](GNS124_U2_T6#GNS124_U2_T6_h5)

question: At what exact moment during patient care should you sort and throw away your waste?

options.A: At the end of the nursing shift
options.B: When the cleaning crew arrives
options.C: Inside the main hospital furnace room
options.D: Immediately at the point of generation

explanation: Always sort waste right where you use it! Doing it immediately stops accidental mixing and keeps everyone safe from needle pricks later.

question: What is a practical public health strategy used to boost local food availability?

options.A: Encouraging families to stop buying fresh fruits and vegetables
options.B: Increasing taxes on food items sold in urban supermarkets
options.C: Closing down smallholder farms to build larger hospitals
options.D: Establishing community food banks and improving rural roads

explanation: Better roads and food banks help supplies move safely and reach communities that need them most. Excellent practical knowledge!

question: What are the normal blood vessels found inside a healthy newborn umbilical cord?

options.A: Two arteries and one vein
options.B: Three arteries and two veins
options.C: Two veins and one artery
options.D: One artery and one vein

explanation: Think 'AVA': Artery, Vein, Artery (two arteries, one vein). Finding this normal trio is a great reassuring sign during assessment!

question: Which system in the body pumps out stress hormones like cortisol and adrenaline when you face a sudden scare?

options.A: The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis
options.B: The lymphatic fluid drainage system
options.C: The gastrointestinal digestive tract
options.D: The superficial integumentary system

explanation: It is a big mouthful to say, but the HPA axis is your body's master alarm system for stress. It floods your system with cortisol to get you ready for action!

question: What is orthostatic hypotension?

options.A: A gradual increase in systolic pressure during physical exercise
options.B: A permanent resting heart rate drop below fifty beats per minute
options.C: An acute spike in blood pressure caused by emotional stress
options.D: A sudden drop in blood pressure when moving from sitting to standing

explanation: Spot on! It's that dizzy feeling when you jump out of bed too quickly because your blood vessels didn't constrict fast enough to keep blood in your brain.

question: What is a nurse assessing when checking a patient's neurological status during an exam?

options.A: The presence of bowel sounds in four quadrants
options.B: Orientation, reflexes, and overall mental function
options.C: The strength and rhythm of the apical pulse
options.D: The rate of air exchange in the lower lung lobes

explanation: Neurological checks look at brain function, nerve responses, and sensory processing to ensure the nervous system is working properly. [learn more](GNS123_U2_T3#GNS123_U2_T3_h6)

question: What are the elevated ridges on the surface of the cerebrum called?

options.A: Sulci
options.B: Ventricles
options.C: Fissures
options.D: Gyri

explanation: Gyri are the raised folds or ridges of brain tissue, while sulci are the shallow grooves between them. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T7#GNS211_U3_T7_h2)

question: Why is it important to let a hot sterilized pack cool down inside the autoclave before touching it?

options.A: Hot metal instruments will bend out of shape if exposed to room air
options.B: The packaging material will immediately catch fire if moved too quickly
options.C: Cooling down resets the chemical indicator strip color back to normal
options.D: Touching it while hot can draw moisture through the wrapper and contaminate the contents

explanation: Touching a hot, damp pack creates condensation. Water droplets act like an elevator for bacteria, letting them slip right through the wrapper!

question: Why must nurses shift their focus from curing to optimizing health when caring for patients with permanent physical disabilities?

options.A: Because chronic conditions rarely respond to any nursing interventions at all
options.B: Because hospital policies prohibit long-term treatment plans for chronic illnesses
options.C: Because patients prefer to manage their own healthcare without professional assistance
options.D: Because many physical impairments are irreversible, making functional independence the primary goal

explanation: When an impairment cannot be reversed, nursing care prioritizes maximizing independence, comfort, and quality of life instead of a cure. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T9#GNS225_U5_T9_h1)

question: A clinic team wants to reduce patient wait times. Which of the following is the best aim statement?

options.A: We will decrease average patient wait time in triage from 45 minutes to under 20 minutes within three months
options.B: We will eliminate all waiting time completely starting next Monday morning
options.C: We will make patients much happier by making the waiting room faster and cleaner
options.D: We will try our best to get patients seen by a doctor before the end of the shift

explanation: Brilliant! This statement is clear because it gives a specific goal, compares it to where you started, and sets a deadline.

question: What is the best way to communicate with a patient experiencing memory issues or confusion?

options.A: Use short, simple sentences and ask one question at a time
options.B: Ask multiple questions at once to save time
options.C: Avoid speaking to the patient and talk only to the wall
options.D: Argue with the patient whenever they become confused

explanation: Keep it brief and sweet! Asking too many things at once can easily overwhelm someone who is dealing with cognitive decline.

question: Why should nurses be involved when high-level health decisions are being made?

options.A: It allows nurses to manage hospital finances without auditing
options.B: It ensures policies reflect practical realities of patient care
options.C: It guarantees that doctors will no longer work in hospitals
options.D: It stops the government from spending money on medication

explanation: Spot on! When nurses have a seat at the table, the resulting rules make sense for everyday clinical work.

question: Why must a stroke client pass a swallow test before you give them normal food?

options.A: To check if the client has an allergy to hospital cutlery
options.B: To prevent food from entering the airway and causing aspiration pneumonia
options.C: To ensure the stomach can digest heavy proteins and fats
options.D: To find out which specific food flavors the client prefers to eat

explanation: Stroke weakness can make throat muscles sluggish, meaning food or water can easily slip down the 'wrong pipe' into the lungs instead of the belly.

question: Why must a nurse figure out if a patient's bone or joint problem is an acute injury or a long-term chronic condition?

options.A: Chronic conditions always require immediate emergency surgery
options.B: Chronic conditions cannot be assessed using standard nursing interviews
options.C: Acute injuries never involve any swelling or localized pain
options.D: Acute injuries and chronic conditions require completely different management approaches

explanation: Spot-on! Knowing whether a problem happened suddenly or built up over time completely changes how you care for and manage the patient.

question: Which part of the syringe driver securely holds the syringe plunger and pushes it forward?

options.A: The clear plastic needle cap
options.B: The external wall power plug
options.C: The claw or drive mechanism
options.D: The digital display screen

explanation: Correct! The drive mechanism (or claw) locks onto the plunger and slowly advances it to deliver the exact dose.

question: What should you do immediately after using a needle to draw blood?

options.A: Carefully scoop the needle cap back on using one hand to prevent injury
options.B: Place the needle on a clean tray until the end of the shift
options.C: Break the needle tip off with forceps before throwing it in the bin
options.D: Drop the unrecapped needle directly into a puncture-resistant sharps container

explanation: Never recap needles! Dropping them straight into the sharps box right beside you is the safest way to avoid accidental needle-pricks.

question: A postoperative patient refuses to eat because food always brings severe belly pain and nausea. What is your best nursing action?

options.A: Administer prescribed pain and anti-nausea medications thirty minutes before the next meal
options.B: Remove all food trays permanently and start total parenteral nutrition
options.C: Force the patient to finish the entire meal tray immediately
options.D: Tell the patient that eating is mandatory for legal discharge

explanation: Brilliant! Managing pain and nausea before mealtime makes eating comfortable so the patient can actually get their nutrition.

question: Why do doctors order a D-dimer blood test when checking for a deep vein thrombosis (DVT)?

options.A: To look for protein fragments that show a recent blood clot is breaking down
options.B: To measure blood pressure inside leg veins
options.C: To see plaque buildup inside the aorta
options.D: To check how fast red blood cells settle in a tube

explanation: D-dimer is a leftover protein piece that floats around when the body is dissolving a blood clot. If the test is negative, it's a great clue that a clot isn't lurking there!

question: Why is signing off at the very end of the monitoring form compulsory?

options.A: It proves that the nursing supervisor worked overtime hours
options.B: It allows the central store to bill individual patients directly
options.C: It serves as a legal waiver for expired medical supplies
options.D: It establishes accountability for the accuracy of the reported data

explanation: You nailed it. A signature means someone is taking responsibility to verify that the numbers written down are actually correct.

question: How do barrier methods like condoms actually prevent STIs?

options.A: To permanently neutralize circulating viral loads in the bloodstream
options.B: To increase local mucosal immunity against parasitic invasion
options.C: To block the exchange of infectious bodily fluids during intercourse
options.D: To destroy bacterial cell walls upon contact in the vaginal canal

explanation: You got it! Condoms act as a physical shield so infectious fluids don't pass between partners.

question: What particle size is generally needed for medication to reach the deep lower airways and alveoli?

options.A: Between 50 and 100 micrometers
options.B: Greater than 20 micrometers
options.C: Between 1 and 5 micrometers
options.D: Any visible dust particle size

explanation: Fine particles measuring 1 to 5 micrometers are small enough to bypass the upper airway and settle deep in the bronchioles and alveoli. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h2)

question: What type of water is best for soaking Plaster of Paris bandages?

options.A: Ice cold water
options.B: Boiling hot water
options.C: Carbonated water
options.D: Lukewarm water

explanation: Lukewarm water gives you a predictable setting time. Hot water makes it set way too fast, and cold water slows it right down.

question: Which of these expenses is considered an indirect cost in a hospital?

options.A: Electricity used to light the entire hospital building
options.B: Bandages applied to a specific wound on a patient
options.C: The specific medication prescribed for hypertension
options.D: Surgical instruments sterilized for one specific operation

explanation: General electricity benefits everyone in the hospital, so you can't assign it to just one patient chart. That's why it's indirect!

question: What is the very first step when you want to develop a conceptual framework?

options.A: Drawing boxes and arrows on a whiteboard
options.B: Publishing the final research paper
options.C: Reviewing the existing literature on the topic
options.D: Collecting blood samples from patients

explanation: You always start by reading what other researchers have already discovered so you know what factors matter most for your topic.

question: Why does the body redirect blood away from the skin and intestines during early shock?

options.A: To prevent the kidneys from producing urine
options.B: To prioritize blood supply for the heart and brain
options.C: To increase the absorption of oral fluids
options.D: To cool down the body temperature quickly

explanation: Shunting redirects scarce blood from less vital areas like the skin and gut to vital organs that cannot survive without constant perfusion. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T2#GNS221_U3_T2_h2)

question: Why should you avoid fancy 3D effects when making pie charts?

options.A: They make the computer file size too large to email
options.B: They prevent the calculation of correct degrees
options.C: They distort perspective and make slice sizes misleading
options.D: Journals charge extra fees for color graphics

explanation: Spot on! 3D tilting makes some slices look bigger than they actually are, which tricks the reader.

question: Why is wearing a medical alert bracelet so important for someone with hypoadrenalism?

options.A: It prevents the patient from developing secondary infections
options.B: It alerts emergency workers to their need for stress-dose steroids
options.C: It reminds the patient to take their daily morning pills
options.D: It measures blood sugar levels continuously throughout the day

explanation: If an emergency happens and the patient can't speak, the bracelet tells paramedics right away that they need life-saving steroids immediately.

question: Which of the following is NOT a common complication of chronic hypochondriasis?

options.A: Financial stress from excessive medical appointments
options.B: Risks from unnecessary invasive medical procedures
options.C: Strain on marital and family relationships
options.D: Permanent physical immunity to all infectious diseases

explanation: You got it! Illness anxiety definitely doesn't give you superpower immunity; instead, it brings relationship strain, money troubles, and risks from needless procedures.

question: Why is telling a worried patient 'everything will be fine' considered a poor communication habit?

options.A: It forces the patient to take extra medication
options.B: It dismisses the patient's genuine emotional distress
options.C: It violates hospital administrative laws
options.D: It lowers the patient's blood pressure too quickly

explanation: Offering false reassurance shuts down conversation. It brushes off their real fears instead of letting them safely express what's bothering them.

question: What is a major advantage of community-based mental health programs?

options.A: They completely remove the need for any professional medical staff
options.B: They require patients to live inside locked hospital facilities
options.C: They keep patients connected to their families and local neighborhoods
options.D: They eliminate all symptoms of mental illness permanently

explanation: Community-based care allows individuals to receive treatment while staying integrated in their daily social and family environments. [learn more](GNS314_U5_T1#GNS314_U5_T1_h7)

question: How did healthcare delivery change globally after Primary Health Care was introduced?

options.A: It focused exclusively on building high-tech specialist hospitals in rural areas
options.B: It transferred all health responsibilities away from governments to private individuals
options.C: It eliminated traditional medicine entirely in favor of imported pharmaceuticals
options.D: It shifted from expensive hospital-centric curative care to community-based preventive care

explanation: You got it! Before PHC, the system waited for people to fall sick and travel far to hospitals. PHC changed this by bringing prevention and basic care directly to the people.

question: You are starting a new maternal health project in a rural village. What should be your very first step when designing its monitoring plan?

options.A: Purchase expensive computer servers for data storage
options.B: Discontinue all existing paper health registers immediately
options.C: Define the main goals and objectives of the health program
options.D: Hire international consultants to write the final evaluation report

explanation: You can't measure your progress until you clearly know what the project is trying to achieve first!

question: To renew her practicing license, a nurse must show she attended approved professional workshops. What policy makes this happen?

options.A: Automatic hospital promotion schemes
options.B: International migration clearance guidelines
options.C: Basic nursing apprenticeship criteria
options.D: Mandatory continuing professional development

explanation: Spot on! Continuing professional development (CPD) ensures we keep learning and sharpening our skills throughout our careers.

question: What are the three main pillars that make up evidence-based practice?

options.A: Patient age, family background, and disease diagnosis
options.B: Research evidence, clinical expertise, and patient values
options.C: Hospital policy, physician orders, and insurance budgets
options.D: Textbook theory, nursing tradition, and administrative rules

explanation: EBP is a balanced approach that requires combining valid research findings with the nurse's professional judgment and what matters to the patient. [learn more](GNS217_U2_T5#GNS217_U2_T5_h3)

question: Why did health experts lower the amount of sugar in the standard ORS formula over time?

options.A: To save manufacturing costs for pharmaceutical companies
options.B: To make the powder dissolve faster in contaminated water
options.C: To stop children from developing diabetes during illness
options.D: To prevent excess sugar from pulling extra water back into the gut

explanation: Too much sugar actually acts like a sponge, drawing water back out into the stool. Lowering the sugar keeps the fluid moving safely into the body instead!

question: Why shouldn't you give anti-bleeding (antihaemorrhagic) drugs to a patient who already has active blood clots?

options.A: It lowers their blood pressure too quickly
options.B: It stops the liver from making albumin
options.C: It prevents the kidneys from filtering urine
options.D: It can cause dangerous new clots in vital organs

explanation: If a patient is already forming unwanted clots, giving drugs that promote clotting is like pouring fuel on a fire—it can cause dangerous blockages!

question: What should a nurse researcher do if their new results don't match older studies?

options.A: Hide the contradictory data so the paper gets published
options.B: Explore potential reasons for the differences in findings
options.C: Change the original hypothesis to match the old literature
options.D: Assume all previous researchers made mistakes in math

explanation: Exactly! Science grows when we look closely at *why* results differ—maybe times have changed, or the patient group is different.

question: What happens to the body when someone goes without sleep for too long?

options.A: Sensory processing becomes sharper
options.B: Muscle mass grows automatically
options.C: Immune function becomes compromised
options.D: Metabolic rate permanently increases

explanation: Missing sleep puts stress on your body and wears down your immune defenses. Remember to get some rest during exam prep week!

question: In rehabilitation terms, how is a 'handicap' different from an 'impairment'?

options.A: An impairment is always caused by poverty
options.B: An impairment cannot be treated by nurses
options.C: A handicap is the social disadvantage resulting from a disability
options.D: A handicap refers strictly to internal organ failure

explanation: Think of an impairment as the physical body change, while a handicap is how that change creates hurdles in everyday social roles and activities. Keep pushing forward!

question: Why is a pelvic ultrasound ordered for a patient with severe pelvic pain and suspected oophoritis?

options.A: To look at the ovaries and check for abscesses or fluid
options.B: To completely replace the need for a physical exam
options.C: To check the length of the patient's menstrual cycle
options.D: To measure exact hormone levels in the blood

explanation: Ultrasounds give us a clear 'window' inside the pelvis to spot structural changes or dangerous pockets of fluid like abscesses.

question: A Lassa fever patient's urine output drops to 15 mL/hour over two hours. What should you do first?

options.A: Document the finding as normal for viral infections and recheck in eight hours
options.B: Encourage the patient to drink large volumes of plain water quickly
options.C: Stop all intravenous fluid infusions to give the kidneys a rest
options.D: Notify the doctor immediately and assess for developing kidney compromise

explanation: Low urine output is a red flag for acute kidney injury. Always report it promptly so the medical team can adjust care.

question: Why might a patient with a badly damaged kidney have clear urine with no blood at all?

options.A: The blood supply or ureter to that kidney may be completely blocked or torn.
options.B: Blood from the injury goes directly into the stomach instead of the bladder.
options.C: The other healthy kidney absorbs all the blood before it reaches the urine.
options.D: The kidneys stop producing blood completely after a sudden physical impact.

explanation: If the tube carrying urine (the ureter) or the main blood vessel gets completely torn off, urine and blood from that injured kidney cannot flow down into the bladder. Makes sense, right?

question: What exactly is an occupational health hazard?

options.A: The personal medical history of a factory worker
options.B: Only physical injuries sustained during a night shift
options.C: A financial loss experienced by a business owner
options.D: Any workplace factor that can cause injury or illness

explanation: Think of an occupational hazard as anything at work—like dust, noise, or stress—that can harm a worker's body or mind. You've got this!

question: What is the main purpose of using non-pharmacological comfort measures alongside prescription drugs?

options.A: To reduce the patient's blood pressure back to normal baseline levels
options.B: To completely replace the need for any chemical or opioid medications
options.C: To distract the healthcare team while real medical procedures happen
options.D: To enhance overall relief and give the patient a sense of personal control

explanation: Non-pharmacological methods complement medical therapy by soothing the nervous system and empowering patients to actively manage their comfort. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T14#GNS321_U4_T14_h5)

question: During data screening, which of these findings is clearly wrong and needs immediate fixing?

options.A: A slight variation in the average age of study volunteers
options.B: A missing response on a secondary satisfaction survey question
options.C: A patient heart rate recorded as 1,200 beats per minute
options.D: A normal demographic spread of male and female participants

explanation: Great catch! A human heart rate of 1,200 beats per minute is physically impossible and points to a simple data entry typo. [learn more](GNS224_U2_T1#GNS224_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is the main goal of mental health promotion?

options.A: Building positive emotional strength and well-being
options.B: Treating severe psychiatric disorders with medication
options.C: Managing acute crisis behaviors in the emergency room
options.D: Discharging stable patients back into the community

explanation: Mental health promotion focuses on enhancing overall emotional well-being and psychological strength rather than treating existing illness. [learn more](GNS314_U5_T1#GNS314_U5_T1_h1)

question: What is the most immediate life-threatening complication that can occur during the third stage of labor?

options.A: Neonatal jaundice
options.B: Postpartum hemorrhage
options.C: Gestational diabetes
options.D: Postpartum depression

explanation: Excessive bleeding after delivery can lead to hypovolemic shock and maternal death within a very short time if not managed urgently. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T15#GNS324_U3_T15_h4)

question: In ward inventory, what does hitting your 'minimum stock level' tell you?

options.A: It is the exact number of items used in a single day
options.B: It is the warning sign that tells you to place a new order
options.C: It is the maximum amount the store can hold
options.D: It shows the total financial budget for the clinic

explanation: That's correct! Think of minimum stock as your alarm bell—when supplies drop to this point, it's time to reorder so you don't run out.

question: Who should you use standard precautions for in the ward?

options.A: All patients receiving care regardless of diagnosis
options.B: Visitors and administrative staff members only
options.C: Patients admitted specifically to isolation wards
options.D: Only patients with confirmed infectious diseases

explanation: Great job! Standard precautions are meant for EVERY patient, every single time. Since we don't always know who might be carrying an infection, treating everyone with these safety rules keeps both you and your patients safe.

question: Which member of the healthcare team is best at helping a patient relearn everyday tasks like bathing, dressing, and cooking?

options.A: Occupational therapist
options.B: Speech pathologist
options.C: Respiratory therapist
options.D: Physical therapist

explanation: You're doing fantastic! Occupational therapists focus on daily 'occupations'—helping patients gain independence with self-care tasks so they can get back to living their lives.

question: What is the single biggest preventable cause of chronic lung disease (COPD) worldwide?

options.A: Childhood asthma attacks
options.B: Inhaling coal dust at work
options.C: Smoke from indoor cooking fires
options.D: Tobacco smoke exposure

explanation: Tobacco smoke is tough on the airways and air sacs over time. Because people can choose to avoid or quit it, it stands out as the number one preventable cause of COPD globally.

question: What protein makes up the thick filaments in a sarcomere?

options.A: Tropomyosin
options.B: Myosin
options.C: Actin
options.D: Troponin

explanation: Thick filaments are composed of the protein myosin, which features small heads that pull on thin actin filaments. [learn more](GNS121_U3_T9#GNS121_U3_T9_h4)

question: Which of these is NOT a core nursing responsibility for a patient on targeted receptor therapy?

options.A: Performing surgery to remove the endocrine glands
options.B: Providing emotional support for distressing physical side effects
options.C: Monitoring the patient closely for side effects related to hormone blockade
options.D: Educating the patient on the importance of taking medications regularly

explanation: Surgeons handle the operating room; nurses shine in assessment, patient education, emotional care, and managing side effects. You've got this! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T11#GNS211_U1_T11_h7)

question: Why are community health nurses in a great position to spot children at risk of delinquency?

options.A: They possess the exclusive legal authority to arrest young lawbreakers
options.B: They interact with families across homes, schools, and clinics regularly
options.C: They spend most of their working hours inside maximum-security prisons
options.D: They are the only healthcare workers trained in psychological diagnosis

explanation: Spot on! Because nurses visit homes, schools, and clinics, they see family dynamics firsthand and can catch early warning signs.

question: A doctor orders a pain relief pill marked 'prn'. When should you give this drug?

options.A: Every four hours exactly on the clock
options.B: Only when the patient reports pain
options.C: Twice daily regardless of symptoms
options.D: Right before the patient eats breakfast

explanation: Exactly! 'prn' stands for 'pro re nata', meaning 'as needed'. You give it when the patient's symptoms call for it, like asking for pain relief.

question: What happens in the colon when someone doesn't drink enough water?

options.A: Peristalsis becomes dangerously fast and watery
options.B: Gastric acid production increases rapidly
options.C: The colon extracts more water, causing hard and dry stool
options.D: The colon stops absorbing nutrients completely

explanation: When the body is short on water, the colon tries to save every drop by sucking extra moisture out of the waste, leading to dry, hard stools.

question: What is the main goal of introducing a new idea for change in healthcare?

options.A: Lowering the salaries of clinical staff
options.B: Increasing the administrative workload of nurses
options.C: Reducing the total number of hospital beds
options.D: Improving care delivery and patient outcomes
